An initiative can be delivered successfully, meet its milestones, and still leave an organisation with a problem it hasn’t fully solved. I encountered this distinction during a digital transformation initiative where an existing solution was expected to support a broader portfolio of products and customer experiences. While the initial implementation met its immediate objectives, extending the same approach would have introduced increasing development duplication, testing effort, and long-term maintenance costs. The challenge wasn’t simply to extend the existing solution. It was to reconsider whether the underlying approach could support the organisation’s longer-term ambitions. I helped challenge the original direction and shape an alternative that prioritised reusability, flexibility, and sustainable delivery across multiple products. The objective was to enable future capabilities to be delivered more efficiently, reduce unnecessary duplication, and preserve the flexibility needed to address different business requirements. It reinforced a lesson that has stayed with me throughout my engineering leadership career: Building something successfully and building something that creates sustainable business value are not necessarily the same thing. Completing Stanford Online’s From Product Strategy to Product Leadership specialisation through Coursera brought this distinction into sharper focus. The programme reinforced the connection between product strategy, technology investment, organisational effectiveness, and the decisions leaders make as businesses evolve. A roadmap explains what we intend to build. Strategy explains why. Technology organisations invest considerable effort in planning, prioritisation, and predictable execution. These disciplines matter. They provide clarity, enable coordination, and make delivery more manageable. But an organisation can deliver its entire roadmap and still struggle to demonstrate meaningful business value. Sometimes the issue isn’t how effectively the work was delivered. It’s whether the right work was chosen in the first place. In my experience, some of the most consequential decisions emerge when teams challenge the assumptions behind an initiative rather than concentrating solely on its immediate requirements. Will the investment remain valuable as the organisation grows? Does it create capabilities that can be reused? Are we solving a recurring business problem or introducing another layer of complexity? What opportunities are we choosing not to pursue? These questions shift the conversation from delivery commitments to strategic choices. And they highlight an important distinction: A roadmap should reflect strategy, not substitute for it. At scale, customer experience and risk become inseparable One of the recurring challenges in enterprise technology is balancing customer convenience, security, operational resilience, and commercial priorities. These considerations are often presented as competing objectives. In one initiative, the business wanted to make the customer experience significantly more convenient by reducing unnecessary interruptions during ongoing interactions. The objective was reasonable and aligned with improving customer experience. However, implementing the requirement without sufficient consideration of the associated risks could have introduced unintended consequences. Rather than treating the discussion as a choice between convenience and protection, we worked towards an approach that preserved the intended experience while maintaining appropriate safeguards. The most important part of that decision wasn’t a particular technology or implementation method. It was recognising that the original requirement described a desired experience, not necessarily the most appropriate way to achieve it. That distinction created room for a better solution. It also reinforced something I believe is fundamental to senior technology leadership. A stakeholder’s proposed solution and the business outcome they want to achieve are not always the same thing. Understanding the difference allows teams to challenge assumptions constructively without losing sight of the original objective. Good decision-making isn’t about choosing between competing priorities. It’s about understanding the trade-offs and finding a responsible path towards the intended outcome. Sometimes the greatest improvement is removing a dependency Product and technology improvements are often associated with introducing new capabilities, modernising systems, or accelerating delivery. Yet some of the most meaningful improvements happen when organisations rethink how work gets done. In one operational environment, a range of routine requests depended on specialist engineering teams, even when those activities did not require extensive technical investigation. This created avoidable dependencies, increased resolution times, and diverted engineering capacity from work requiring deeper technical expertise.
